stories.title: AI Companies Sign Full-Floor Leases at Repositioned Flatiron District Building
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged two full-floor office leases totaling 16,734 square feet at 61 W. 23rd St. in Manhattan’s Flatiron District, bringing the recently repositioned property to full occupancy. AI companies Normal Computing and Inspiren have each leased an entire floor at the building. Normal Computing’s space will become its new headquarters in New York City. Connor Daugstrup of Cushman & Wakefield represented ownership in both transactions. Normal Computing was represented by Gabe Marans and Maxine Rosen of Savills. Inspiren was represented by Adam Spector and Ally Krieger of Newmark. Ownership was also advised by George Tsapelas from Taconic Development Advisors.   “It’s notable to see two fast-growing AI companies independently arrive at the same conclusion and commit to full-floor spaces at 61 West 23rd Street,” said Daugstrup. “For companies competing for highly skilled talent, the office remains an important part of the growth equation. These leases reflect the continued appeal of Midtown South and the demand we’re seeing from innovative firms that want space capable of supporting their next stage of growth.” The post AI Companies Sign Full-Floor Leases at Repositioned Flatiron District Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Normal Computing, Inspiren lease 16,734 sf full floors at 61 W. 23rd, Flatiron.
Normal Computing relocates NYC HQ, plans to double NY headcount from ~30 employees.
AI talent war driving office demand in Midtown South despite broader office weakness.
stories.summary: Two AI firms—Normal Computing and Inspiren—signed full-floor leases totaling 16,734 square feet at 61 West 23rd Street in Manhattan's Flatiron District, bringing the repositioned building to full occupancy. Normal Computing is relocating and expanding its NYC headquarters, currently at 5,250 sf three blocks south, with plans to hire enough to double its New York headcount. The leases signal continued office demand from fast-growing tech firms competing for skilled talent in Midtown South.
stories.impact: AI and high-growth tech demand for premium office space in Manhattan creates a magnet for knowledge-worker inflow and signals a localized, talent-driven rent floor in Flatiron/Midtown South—even as office fundamentals soften citywide. Multifamily developers should monitor tech employment hubs (especially AI, fintech, biotech clusters) as leading indicators of residential demand and rent growth in proximate neighborhoods; Normal Computing's headcount doubling plan suggests upstream demand for workforce housing in Manhattan below $4k/month.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges Valencia Office Sale for Harbor Associates
stories.excerpt: CBRE facilitated the $32-million sale of Commons at Valencia, a two-building Class A office campus totaling approximately 157,189 square feet, located at 25124 and 25152 Springfield Court in Valencia. Strauss Investments LLC acquired the property from Harbor Associates. The CBRE team of Mark Shaffer, Anthony DeLorenzo, Sean Sullivan and Gerard Poutier represented Harbor Associates. “Commons at Valencia attracted significant investor interest due to its strong tenant roster, recent capital improvements and strategic location within one of Southern California’s premier suburban office markets,” said Shaffer. “The property’s leasing momentum and long-term growth prospects within the Valencia submarket created a compelling investment opportunity for the buyer.” Originally built in 2005, Commons at Valencia consists of two three-story office buildings and a two-story parking structure with 625 parking spaces. At the time of sale, the property was 79% occupied by a diverse roster of professional services, insurance, financial services and real estate tenants. The post CBRE Arranges Valencia Office Sale for Harbor Associates appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Strauss Investments buys Commons at Valencia office for $32M from Harbor Associates.
157,189 sf class-A, two-building campus 79% occupied, built 2005, Valencia submarket.
Office asset sale signals investor appetite for stabilized suburban California flex/office.
stories.summary: CBRE facilitated the $32 million sale of Commons at Valencia, a 157,189-square-foot, two-building Class A office campus in Valencia, Southern California, to Strauss Investments LLC from Harbor Associates. The property was 79% occupied at sale with diverse tenancy (professional services, insurance, financial services, real estate) and had recently undergone capital improvements. The transaction reflects investor interest in well-located suburban office with leasing momentum and growth prospects.
stories.impact: Modest relevance to multifamily development. Office sales in suburban SoCal do not directly signal residential demand; however, a 79%-occupied, circa-2005 office asset trading suggests institutional capital is still picking at lower-basis office—not signaling broad repricing that would unlock land or development sites for residential conversion in Valencia submarket. Monitor only if asset is adjacent to mixed-use or residential development opportunity.

stories.title: Japanese Firm Acquires Upper West Side Apartments for $25M
stories.excerpt: Alchemy Ventures announced the sale of 310 W. 80th St., a 36-unit residential elevator building on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, to Japan-based Phoenix Co. Ltd. for $24.8 million. Alchemy originally acquired the property in February 2024 for $11.2 million, with the sale representing a significant increase from the company’s acquisition price after a gut renovation. Ian Brooks, Robert Shapiro, Nicholas Kontos, and David Garcia of CBRE handled the deal for Alchemy Ventures.The sale is part of Alchemy Ventures’ ongoing strategy of acquiring, operating and selectively monetizing residential and mixed-use properties throughout New York City “310 West 80th Street was a great example of the type of residential asset we look for at Alchemy Ventures: well-located, fundamentally strong properties in established New York City neighborhoods,” said Sam Kooris, principal/co-founder “The transaction reflects our continued focus on identifying opportunities, creating value through hands-on ownership and management, and strategically realizing that value as we continue to grow and evolve our portfolio.” The post Japanese Firm Acquires Upper West Side Apartments for $25M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Phoenix Co. Ltd. (Japan) acquires 36-unit UWS elevator building for $24.8M.
Alchemy Ventures bought same asset Feb 2024 for $11.2M, gut-renovated, 121% gain.
Foreign capital targeting stabilized NYC multifamily; value-add playbook still works for quick flip.
stories.summary: Alchemy Ventures sold 310 West 80th Street, a 36-unit elevator building on Manhattan's Upper West Side, to Japan-based Phoenix Co. Ltd. for $24.8 million—just 10 months after acquiring it for $11.2 million in February 2024. The gain reflects value creation through gut renovation and repositioning. Alchemy's strategy centers on acquiring, operating, and selectively monetizing residential assets in NYC neighborhoods.
stories.impact: Japanese and foreign capital continues to view stabilized, value-add NYC multifamily (especially UWS) as a core hold and wealth-store, validating limited supply of prime pre-war stock. For Trammell Crow, this signals: (1) exit windows remain attractive for stabilized/renovated assets in strong neighborhoods, (2) competition for acquisition targets will remain fierce from international players with low cost-of-capital, and (3) NYC residential cap rates and entry valuations are unlikely to compress further—focus on value-add and core-plus repositioning rather than stabilized core buys.

stories.title: Victoria Industrial, Lincoln Equities Buy NoVa Industrial Portfolio for $63M
stories.excerpt: Victoria Industrial Properties and Lincoln Equities Group have acquired a seven-building flex industrial portfolio in Northern Virginia’s Dulles Tech Corridor for $62.5 million. Baltimore-based Klein Enterprises sold the assets. The portfolio includes a two-building, 67,000-square-foot property at 380 and 400 Herndon Parkway in Herndon; a 95,000-square-foot building at 45745 Nokes Boulevard in Sterling; and four buildings combining for 150,000 square feet in Chantilly’s Sullyfield Business Park. The Business Journals reported the sale. The properties are leased to a mix of defense, medical, government consulting and service tenants. Honeywell and defense-tech firm Artis anchor the Herndon assets, while the Sterling property houses Inova’s blood donor facility as well as defense contractors Nightwing and Capital Electric. “We are incredibly bullish on the Dulles corridor’s flex industrial market,” Victoria Industrial Properties founder Jacob Schulder said in a statement. He pointed to the region’s data center industry and related tenant demand as major drivers. Klein acquired the properties separately between 2019 and 2020. The sale comes as the company shifts its focus toward grocery-anchored retail and multifamily, according to President Daniel Klein. Northern Virginia’s data center expansion is also putting pressure on industrial supply. Klein Chief Investment Officer Sean Garland said rents across the firm’s flex and industrial holdings have benefited from limited land, rising replacement costs and competition from data center development. That has helped fuel a wave of industrial activity across the region. J.E. Richards recently signed a nearly 1 million-square-foot lease described as the largest industrial lease between the D.C. metro area and Richmond. TA Realty also paid $132 million for a 13-building Woodbridge industrial park in July, while theSilverman Group acquired a 1.4 million-square-foot Maryland and Virginia portfolio for $203 million earlier
bullets: Victoria Industrial, Lincoln Equities buy 312,000 sf flex portfolio in Dulles for $62.5M.
Seven buildings across Herndon, Sterling, Chantilly; anchored by Honeywell, Artis, Inova, defense contractors.
Northern Virginia defense-tech, data-center cluster driving flex industrial demand and valuations.
stories.summary: Victoria Industrial Properties and Lincoln Equities Group acquired a seven-building flex industrial portfolio totaling approximately 312,000 square feet across Northern Virginia's Dulles Tech Corridor for $62.5 million from Klein Enterprises. Assets are leased to defense, medical, government consulting, and service tenants, including anchors Honeywell, Artis (defense-tech), Inova, and defense contractors Nightwing and Capital Electric. The purchasers cited the region's data center industry and related tenant demand as major growth drivers.
stories.impact: Northern Virginia's defense, federal contracting, and emerging data-center ecosystem are pulling industrial real estate capital and supporting tight flex space—a leading indicator of corporate employment clustering and white-collar inflow to the NoVA corridor. Multifamily developers should monitor Dulles submarket (Herndon, Sterling, Chantilly, Ashburn) for secondary/tertiary office and tech hubs driving workforce migration; data-center operations and defense-tech growth support sustained job formation and rental demand for workforce/workforce-plus housing in suburban NoVA through 2025–2027.

stories.title: Hoag Hospital Opens $1B Expansion in Irvine
stories.excerpt: Hoag on Monday announced the opening of the Hoag Hospital Irvine Sun Family Campus, a $1-billion expansion that brings specialized hospitals, outpatient facilities, advanced surgical services and nationally recognized clinical programs together on one integrated campus in Irvine. The expansion adds six new buildings to the hospital campus, as well as 155 inpatient beds, bringing the hospital’s total bed count to 251. It includes 120,000 square feet of ambulatory facilities, along with Orange County’s first dedicated Cancer Urgent Care. “This expansion is more than a collection of state-of-the-art buildings. It reflects Hoag’s commitment to growing alongside Orange County, while continuing to redefine what healthcare can look like,” said Robert T. Braithwaite, president & CEO of Hoag. “The Hoag Hospital Irvine Sun Family Campus was envisioned as a healthcare village, bringing specialized care and clinical expertise together in a place where every aspect of the patient experience was designed to make care more connected, more convenient, and more personalized.” The post Hoag Hospital Opens $1B Expansion in Irvine appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hoag Hospital opens $1B expansion in Irvine with 155 new inpatient beds, 6 buildings.
Brings total bed count to 251; 120,000 sf ambulatory, cancer urgent care, integrated campus.
Major employer capex and workforce expansion; healthcare service-area demand driver for OC.
stories.summary: Hoag Hospital announced the opening of the Hoag Hospital Irvine Sun Family Campus, a $1 billion expansion adding six new buildings, 155 inpatient beds (total now 251), 120,000 square feet of ambulatory facilities, and Orange County's first dedicated cancer urgent care. The campus consolidates specialized hospitals, outpatient services, and surgical centers on one integrated site.
stories.impact: Irvine's largest healthcare expansion in years signals sustained population and service-area demand in Orange County; Hoag's capital deployment and likely hiring of 200–400+ clinical and support staff creates direct employment and inbound worker migration. For Trammell Crow, monitor Irvine/Tustin submarket (and OC more broadly) for secondary job growth, wage stability, and workforce-housing absorption near Hoag campus and surrounding medical corridors; healthcare job creation is non-cyclical and supports renter purchasing power and pricing power in Irvine and adjacent areas.

stories.title: Walker & Dunlop Arranges $86M Refi for Flushing Affordable Quartet
stories.excerpt: Walker & Dunlop arranged an $86,443,000 Freddie Mac refinancing of a 506-unit multifamily portfolio in the Flushing neighborhood of Queens. The loan was originated on behalf of Iris Holdings Group, a national affordable housing preservation and investment firm, and refinances the portfolio’s existing debt while supporting its long-term affordability. The Flushing Preservation Portfolio is comprised of four elevator buildings at 44-15, 45-15 and 45-35 Colden St. and 137-20 45th Ave. The 481,000-square-foot portfolio features covered parking, views of Kissena Corridor Park and features a mix of studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom units. Iris Holdings Group partnered with the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development in 2024 to preserve this project at varying levels of affordability for the next 40 years. Walker & Dunlop Affordable Housing Debt and Capital Markets Real Estate Finance, led by John Gilmore and Harvey Pava, arranged the fixed-rate financing. The post Walker & Dunlop Arranges $86M Refi for Flushing Affordable Quartet appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Walker & Dunlop arranges $86.4M Freddie Mac refi for 506-unit Flushing affordable portfolio.
Four-building, 481,000 sf elevator properties; 40-year affordability covenant via HPD partnership.
Freddie Mac liquidity enabling preservation of affordable inventory in tight Queens market.
stories.summary: Walker & Dunlop arranged an $86.443 million Freddie Mac refinancing of a 506-unit affordable multifamily portfolio in Flushing, Queens, on behalf of Iris Holdings Group. The Flushing Preservation Portfolio comprises four elevator buildings totaling 481,000 square feet and is preserved at varying affordability levels for 40 years through partnership with NYC's Department of Housing Preservation and Development. The fixed-rate financing supports long-term affordability preservation.
stories.impact: Freddie Mac's active lending into affordable preservation reflects sustained GSE appetite for QSR (Qualified Support Resources) and LIHTC-backed deals; Flushing's tight rental market and robust immigration-driven demand support affordability preservation economics. For Trammell Crow, this signals: (1) affordable financing windows remain open for value-add and preservation deals with long-term affordability covenants, and (2) Flushing's constrained supply and demand fundamentals make it a defensive market for workforce-housing development—but entitlements and land availability may limit greenfield opportunity.

stories.title: Private Lender Ascent Expands L.A. Headquarters as It Tops $3.7B in Originations
stories.excerpt: Private real estate lender Ascent Developer Solutions is expanding its Los Angeles headquarters after passing $3.7 billion in originations just over two years after launching. The firm signed a lease for 22,000 square feet at Douglas Emmett’s 15821 Ventura Boulevard in Encino in L.A.’s San Fernando Valley, increasing its footprint by 13,000 square feet. More than 150 employees now work for Ascent, and the firm said the larger headquarters will support both headcount growth and rising transaction volume. The company has also been broadening its geographic reach and lending products. Ascent recently expanded into manufactured housing communities and infill development, and, in July, hired John Richardson as chief credit officer. Richardson is based in the firm’s New England office in Massachusetts, which has nearly doubled its headcount since opening in June. CEO Robert Wasmund founded Ascent in July 2024 with the backing of Elliott Investment Management. The company provides short-term loans for acquisitions, renovations and construction involving single-family, homebuilder and multifamily properties, as well as post-completion bridge financing. The firm also offers revolving lending programs and financing for manufactured housing communities with loans of up to $100 million. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Ascent Developer Solutions leases 22,000 sf at 15821 Ventura Blvd, Encino (SFV).
Private lender tops $3.7B originations in ~2 years; 150+ employees; expanding into manufactured housing.
Non-bank construction lending and acquisition lending demand strong; headcount and footprint expansion signals pipeline.
stories.summary: Private real estate lender Ascent Developer Solutions signed a lease for 22,000 square feet at Douglas Emmett's 15821 Ventura Boulevard in Encino, expanding its L.A. headquarters by 13,000 square feet. The firm has originated $3.7 billion in loans since launching in July 2024 (just over two years), now employs 150+, and has expanded into manufactured housing and infill development. CEO Robert Wasmund founded Ascent with Elliott Investment Management backing.
stories.impact: Explosive growth of non-bank construction and acquisition lending (Ascent's $3.7B originations run-rate, headcount doubling, geographic expansion) signals robust capital availability and strong demand for short-term development financing—a leading indicator that developers are acquiring, renovating, and building at scale. Trammell Crow should view Ascent's expansion as evidence of a well-capitalized lending environment supporting development velocity; monitor Ascent's expansion into manufactured housing and infill as signals of capital chasing alternative product types and market niches with lower acquisition and construction-cost barriers.

stories.title: Two AI Companies Ink Full-Floor Deals at 61 West 23rd Street
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence firms Normal Computing and Inspiren have inked full-floor office leases at 61 West 23rd Street in Manhattan’s Flatiron District. The two deals total 16,734 square feet at the Zegna family- and Taconic Partners-owned building between Fifth Avenue and Avenue of the Americas, according to landlord broker Cushman & Wakefield. C&W’s Connor Daugstrup represented the landlord in both deals alongside Taconic Development Advisors’ George Tsapelas. Normal Computing, which develops AI hardware, took 8,367 square feet at the seven-story building in a relocation and expansion of its New York City headquarters. The company currently occupies 5,250 square feet three blocks south at 27 West 20th Street, a spokesperson for Normal Computing told Commercial Observer, and plans to move to its new home in November. The spokesperson noted that approximately 30 employees will operate from Normal Computing’s new headquarters, with sufficient space to support plans to double its New York headcount over the coming year. Savills’ Gabe Marans and Maxine Rosen negotiated the headquarters lease on behalf of Normal Computing. The other high-tech arrival at 61 West 23rd Street, Inspiren, provides an AI-powered technology platform for senior living communities. Inspiren moved into its 8,367-square-foot space in early September, a company spokesperson told CO, marking its first permanent office in New York City. Previous records place Inspiren’s New York City operations at 19 Morris Avenue in Brooklyn’s Navy Yard. Inspiren was represented by Newmark’s Adam Spector and Ally Krieger. The Zegna family and Taconic acquired 61 West 23rd Street for $65 million in 2016. Taconic was tapped to reposition the building, restoring its historic façade and repositioning its interiors with two new lobbies, modernized elevators and pre-built offices. AI firms anchoring premium Flatiron office; talent competition driving space demand despite office headwinds.
stories.summary: AI firms Normal Computing and Inspiren leased full floors totaling 16,734 square feet at 61 West 23rd Street in Manhattan's Flatiron District (Zegna family and Taconic Partners-owned building). Normal Computing is relocating and expanding its NYC headquarters from 27 West 20th Street (5,250 sf), with approximately 30 current employees and plans to double NYC headcount. The leases demonstrate continued strong office demand from high-growth AI companies targeting talent.
stories.impact: Duplicate of Article 1. See Article 1 analysis: AI talent clustering in Flatiron/Midtown South signals sustained white-collar inflow and residential demand in adjacent neighborhoods (Noho, East Village, Gramercy). Monitor AI/tech employment hubs as leading indicators of workforce-housing absorption and rent growth in Manhattan submarkets.

bullets: Moody's Jeffrey Havsy podcast on CRE risks investors are missing; data, climate, credit signals.
Themes: tenant credit, crime, truck traffic, robotics, physical risk vs. ESG underwriting gaps.
Lender and investor blind spots on property fundamentals beyond cap rates and traditional metrics.
stories.summary: Moody's Analytics CRE practice lead Jeffrey Havsy discusses risks CRE investors and lenders are not pricing in, including data scarcity, tenant credit quality, crime impact, truck traffic patterns, climate and physical risk, and the effects of robotics on industrial real estate valuations. Havsy highlights gaps between traditional property-level underwriting and broader economic, credit, and alternative data signals that drive long-term asset performance.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance. Podcast serves as a reminder that multifamily development underwriting should integrate tenant credit, local crime trends, climate risk (flood, wildfire, heat), and demographic volatility—not just rent growth and occupancy. Developers should cross-check underwriting assumptions on renter creditworthiness, neighborhood safety, and physical risk against Moody's or similar third-party datasets; robotics and supply-chain shifts mentioned for industrial may portend labor-force shifts affecting residential demand in logistics hubs.

stories.title: Principal Asset Management Adds Drew Fung for Debt Role
stories.excerpt: Drew Fung, who led Clarion Partners’ commercial real estate debt investment group for the last 14 years, will be taking on a similar role at Principal Asset Management. Principal appointed Fung as managing director of portfolio management focusing on commercial real estate debt investing, with a big emphasis on high-yield and structured debt strategies, the company announced Monday. He will be based out of New York City and report to Chris Duey, senior managing director at Principal Asset Management. Fung has originated more than $3.5 billion across mezzanine and structured debt investments during his nearly 40-year career, according to Principal. He was an honoree on Commercial Observer’s Power Finance list with Clarion for three straight years from 2022 to 2024. Clarion Partners did not immediately return a request for comment. Prior to arriving at Clarion in 2012, Fung was a managing director at Deutsche Bank for six and a half years leading high-yield debt investments. He also held roles at CWCapital and Lendlease during a CRE finance career that dates back to 1987. Fung is also active at the CRE trade association level as a member of the CRE Finance Council (CREFC), the Mortgage Bankers Association and the Urban Land Institute. He also serves on the steering committee of the National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries/CREFC debt fund index launched in 2023. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Drew Fung joins Principal Asset Management as managing director, CRE debt portfolio.
Fung led Clarion's debt group 14 years, originated $3.5B in mezz/structured debt, NYC-based.
Institutional capital redeploying talent into CRE debt; structured debt appetite signal.
stories.summary: Drew Fung, who led Clarion Partners' commercial real estate debt investment group for 14 years, joined Principal Asset Management as managing director of portfolio management for CRE debt investing, focusing on high-yield and structured debt strategies. Fung has originated over $3.5 billion in mezzanine and structured debt investments across a nearly 40-year career and was named to Commercial Observer's Power Finance list three consecutive years (2022–2024).
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. High-profile debt talent migration from Clarion to Principal reflects institutional appetite for structured and mezz debt in CRE—potentially a signal of capital availability for bridge and construction lending in strong-demand markets. Developers seeking mezz or structured financing should monitor Principal's investment strategy, but this hire is primarily a capital-allocation signal, not a market or demand indicator.
